newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Key facts of British colony Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Key facts of British colony Hong Kong.

text.p: Hong Kong, Britain's last important colony, on Wednesday will name the first post-colonial leader to govern the territory when it reverts to Chinese rule in mid-1997. Here is a profile of the territory.
POPULATION - 6.3 million (census department September 1996), 98 per cent Chinese. The rest are mainly expatriates.
CAPITAL - Victoria, name in abeyance, now called Central.

ARMED FORCES - All armed forces in Hong Kong are at present forces of the British Crown. In mid-1997, all units of the British army, navy and airforce will depart and be replaced by a People's Liberation Army garrison up to 10,000 strong. Internal security will remain the responsibility of the Hong Kong police.
ECONOMY - Since the 1970s, Hong Kong has changed from a manufacturing-based to a service-based economy. Companies moved production to factories in southern China to cut labour costs.

Under a fixed exchange rate system, the Hong Kong dollar has been pegged at 7.80 to one U.S. dollar since 1983. Hong Kong interest rates cannot stray too far from U.S. rates, making it hard for the government and banks to control inflation through interest rate policy. In October, the consumer price index rose 5.4 percent year-on-year, and inflation is predicted to average 6 percent for 1996.

Real per capita Gross Domestic Product (GDP) was US$23,000 in 1995. GDP growth slowed to 4.6 pct in 1995 from 5.4 percent in 1994. Growth continued to slow in early 1996 and is estimated at around 4.5 percent in 1996.

Major industries are ready-to-wear clothes, textiles, basic metals, fabricated metal products and electrical and electronic goods. Major imports are raw materials, semi-manufactures, food and mineral fuels. Tourism was the second largest foreign exchange earner in 1995. Visitor spending totaled HK$72 billion, 12 percent up on 1994, and six percent of Hong Kong's GDP.

MODERN HISTORY - Hong Kong means "Fragrant Harbour" in Chinese. It was wrested by Britain from China in three phases starting in the mid-19th century "opium wars". Hong Kong Island went first, under the Treaty of Nanking in 1842. The Kowloon Peninsula was next, by the 1860 Convention of Peking. The rural New Territories, comprising a mainland area adjacent to Kowloon and 235 islands, was added under a 99-year lease in 1898.
Under these treaties, the New Territories, which comprise the bulk of the territory, would revert to China in 1997.
Sino-British talks on the terms of the handover began in 1982 when China made it known it was intent on resuming sovereignty of the entire territory.

From the 1840s to 1950s, apart from the Japanese military occupation of 1941-45, Hong Kong was mainly a staging post and trans-shipment centre for trade between China and the West. But with the 1950s Korean War and a U.N. embargo on strategic goods to China, most of this trade was cut off and Hong Kong became a manufacturing centre, and later a financing centre.

On December 19, 1984, the Sino-British Joint Declaration, a treaty that agreed that all of Hong Kong would be returned to China at midnight on June 30, 1997, was signed in Beijing. The Basic Law, a mini-constitution for the future Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR), was promulgated by China in 1990.

The Joint Declaration promises Hong Kong will keep its capitalist lifestyle and a high degree of autonomy until 2047. Confidence in that pledge was dented in June 1989 when China's tanks crushed a peaceful democracy movement in Beijing with heavy loss of life. Up to a million Hong Kong people protested, fuelling the growth of Hong Kong's own democracy movement.

Hong Kong's first opposition political party, the United Democrats, was founded in 1990 and later became the Democratic Party. Led by outspoken lawyer Martin Lee, the party and allies swept 16 of 18 contestable seats in the Legislative Council in the first direct polls in September 1991. But they were a minority in the 60-seat body. The other members were still named by the governor or elected by "functional constituencies" built around professional and commercial sectors. Directly elected seats rose to 20 in 1995, when pro-democracy groups took 70 percent of the votes.

In November 1996, a China-controlled panel set up a 400-seat Selection Committee to select Hong Kong's first post-colonial Chief Executive and the 60 members of a provisional legislature that will replace the elected Legislative Council (Legco) on July 1, 1997.
